issues.description: The reported flow of participants does not reconcile. If 468 responded at Time 1 and 450 responded at Time 4, 18 participants—not 16—failed to complete all waves. In addition, subtracting 16 missing-time-point exclusions and 78 data-quality exclusions from 468 gives 374, not the stated final N=372. This creates uncertainty about the analytic sample and exclusion process.
issues.quote: The sample size and retention rates between each measurement time point were as follows: n = 468 nurses responded at time 1; n = 458 responded at time 2 (98% retention rate between T1 and T2); n = 454 responded at time 3 (98% retention rate between T2 and T3); and n = 450 responded at time 4 (98% retention rate between T3 and T4). ... Only participants who completed all four surveys (n = 16 people excluded due to missing time points) and whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality) were included in the final sample. ... This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372.

issues.description: The methods state that the final sample size is N=372, but the main correlation and mediation tables report N=321, and the moderation table reports N=244. The manuscript does not clearly explain why the main mediation analyses excluded 51 additional cases, especially when the main mediation model does not appear to require the moderator with missing data. This undermines reproducibility and interpretation of statistical power and precision.
issues.quote: This resulted in a final sample size of N = 372. ... Note. N = 321. ... Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.description: Patient acuity missingness is acknowledged but not quantified in absolute terms in the methods, and the moderation model drops to N=244. Relative to the stated final N=372, this implies loss of 128 cases, about one-third of the sample, for moderation analyses. No missing-data diagnostics, MCAR/MAR assessment, comparison of retained versus excluded cases, or imputation/FIML strategy is reported. Because patient acuity is central to Hypothesis 3, this threatens validity and may bias the interaction estimate.
issues.quote: Finally, our perceived patient acuity measure had missing data. For missing cases, responses were either left blank (55% of missing values were due to no-response) or the value provided was outside of the expected numerical range (45% of missing values were due to an incorrect response). ... Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.description: Participants who missed an intermediate wave were not invited to later waves, and analyses included only complete cases. This creates monotone missingness by design and can induce selection bias if missingness is related to workload, distress, incivility, or fatigue. The attrition analysis is minimal and does not address excluded poor-quality cases or missing moderator data.
issues.quote: Due to budgetary constraints, participants who did not respond to a measurement period were not invited for subsequent surveys (i.e., a participant who did not complete T2 survey was not sent the link for the T3 or T4 surveys). ... Only participants who completed all four surveys ... were included in the final sample.

issues.subcategory: data-quality exclusion counts do not add up
issues.description: The manuscript reports 78 exclusions for poor data quality but then lists criteria accounting for only 57 exclusions: 56 inconsistent demographics and 1 excessive missingness. The remaining 21 exclusions are unexplained, making the data-cleaning procedure opaque and potentially non-reproducible.
issues.quote: whose responses passed a priori determined data quality checks (n = 78 people excluded for poor data quality) ... Responses were considered failed data quality checks if they had any of the following characteristics: (a) demographic information was not consistent across measurement periods (n = 56 people failed to provide reasonably consistent responses to tenure, gender, and/or age); or (b) missing values exceeded 50% of the questions (n = 1).

issues.description: Recruitment materials reportedly required full-time nurses, but the final sample is described as including part-time and full-time nurses. This discrepancy affects the target population, exposure opportunity, work-hour confounding, and generalizability.
issues.quote: Information about inclusion criteria (working full time in a high-stakes/critical care setting as a nurse) and compensation were also provided along with the link to participate. ... All participants were currently employed as a nurse (part- or full-time), worked more than one shift a week, on average, and routinely worked with high severity/high-risk patients.

issues.description: Eligibility for being a nurse in a high-stakes setting appears to have been verified only by self-report. Given online recruitment, social media posting, personal-network snowballing, and monetary incentives, stronger verification or detailed screening procedures are needed to rule out ineligible or fraudulent participants.
issues.quote: To help ensure that the participants were from healthcare contexts, we highlighted the nursing focus in the recruitment and consent information and directly asked participants if they met the inclusion criteria.

issues.description: The sampling frame is unknown and recruitment relied on flyers, personal networks, social media, and forums. This prevents calculation of a response rate and likely yields a self-selected sample of nurses who are reachable, motivated, or interested in incivility/wellbeing research. Claims about nurses broadly, healthcare workers, or service employees should be more limited.
issues.quote: Although the full population size that was sampled from is unknown ... Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. using three recruitment strategies. First, we dropped off recruitment flyers ... Second, we sent emails to nurses and other healthcare professionals in our personal networks ... Finally, we posted study information and recruitment materials online via personal social network accounts ... nurse/healthcare specific forums or groups within social media networks

issues.description: Participants were recruited through hospitals, departments, professional networks, and online nursing groups, implying possible clustering within hospitals, units, regions, or recruitment channels. The analyses appear to treat observations as independent and do not report cluster-robust standard errors, random effects, or design effects. Shared unit climate, staffing, patient population, and management practices could confound or inflate associations.
issues.quote: Participants were recruited from various hospitals across the U.S. ... At each location, we asked the manager/head of the department to post the fliers in employee common areas ... nurse/healthcare specific forums or groups within social media networks

issues.description: The manuscript does not report key contextual characteristics needed to evaluate or replicate the study, such as unit type distribution, hospital type, region, shift type, nurse-patient ratios, patient volume, or proportion of ICU/ED/OR nurses. These factors are highly relevant to patient acuity, incivility exposure, compassion fatigue, and work hours.
issues.quote: The target population of this research included nurses within healthcare industries, particularly those working in high-stakes or critical care settings. ... All participants ... routinely worked with high severity/high-risk patients.

issues.description: Experienced and enacted incivility were measured as weekly frequencies, but nurses vary in hours worked, number of shifts, number of patients, type of unit, and patient/family contact. Without a denominator such as patient encounters or hours in direct care, higher reported incivility may reflect greater exposure opportunity rather than higher per-contact incivility. Work hours are included inconsistently and patient volume is not measured.
issues.quote: Participants were asked, “Thinking about your experiences at work during the past week, how often have you been in a situation where any of your patients or patient family members/friends…” ... All participants ... worked more than one shift a week, on average

issues.description: Patient acuity is defined as severity of illness and intensity of nursing care, but it is operationalized as a single self-reported percentage of patients considered “severe” across heterogeneous departments and acuity systems. This does not capture care intensity, workload, patient turnover, nurse-patient ratio, or objective acuity, and the meaning of “severe” likely differs across specialties and hospitals.
issues.quote: Patient acuity is defined as “a measure of the severity of illness of the patient and the intensity of nursing care that patient requires” ... we measure the respondents’ perceptions of patient acuity across all patients they attended to within the last work week by asking them to estimate a percentage of their patients that were “severe.”

issues.description: The patient acuity moderator is a newly created single item. No reliability can be estimated, and validity evidence is limited to small pilot feedback. Measurement error in a moderator can attenuate or distort interaction effects, especially with substantial missing/out-of-range responses.
issues.quote: To develop our perceived patient acuity measure, we first discussed patient acuity measurement strategies with our qualitative pilot participants via small focus groups and individual interviews. ... Following the survey development, we tested this new item within the quantitative pilot study.

issues.description: The construct is labeled patient incivility, but the source includes patients, family members, and friends. These sources can differ in motivations, constraints, severity, and nurse response. Combining them prevents conclusions specifically about patient incivility and may obscure different mechanisms.
issues.quote: Within this context, the customers are the patients and their families. The incivility examined is therefore incivility from patients and their families (experienced incivility) and incivility towards patients and their families (enacted incivility).

issues.description: Experienced incivility includes patients and family/friends, but negative emotions are measured only “towards patients.” If incivility was caused by family members, emotions toward patients may not be the relevant mediator. This mismatch weakens the proposed mediation chain.
issues.quote: Participants were asked, “Thinking about your experiences at work during the past week, how often have you been in a situation where any of your patients or patient family members/friends…” ... Participants were asked to rate “How often do you feel the following emotions towards patients”

issues.description: The study treats patients and families as customers, but patient-nurse relationships involve vulnerability, clinical need, legal/ethical duties, impaired capacity, and care-team dynamics that differ from ordinary customer-service exchanges. The manuscript acknowledges this complexity but still generalizes to customer incivility and service industries, which may misapply customer-incivility theory.
issues.quote: We view the patient-nurse relationship as a specialized form of customer-employee relationship. However, it is important to understand that this relationship includes care provision and care coordination, which is more complex and dynamic than some other employee-customer relationships.

issues.subcategory: incivility items may not be valid in clinical context
issues.description: Some adapted WIS items may not indicate incivility in healthcare. For example, patients or families doubting a nurse’s judgment may reflect informed consent, advocacy, fear, confusion, pain, or prior medical experience rather than rude deviance. Conversely, nurses doubting a patient’s judgment may be clinically appropriate in some contexts. This threatens construct validity of both experienced and enacted incivility.
issues.quote: “Doubted your judgment on a matter over which you had responsibility” ... “Doubted one or more patient’s/patient family members’ judgment on a matter over which they had responsibility”

issues.subcategory: compassion fatigue treated as undifferentiated burnout/exhaustion
issues.description: The manuscript defines compassion fatigue as consisting of burnout and secondary trauma and states that either component may constitute compassion fatigue, but then treats the 13-item short scale as a single composite. No subscale analyses or factor structure for this sample are reported. This may conflate distinct constructs with different causes and outcomes.
issues.quote: Compassion fatigue consists of burnout and secondary trauma components, with employees experiencing compassion fatigue if they are experiencing either caregiving-related burnout or secondary trauma (or both of these simultaneously). ... The scale consisted of 13 items

issues.subcategory: weekly timeframe may not match compassion fatigue construct
issues.description: Compassion fatigue is described as progressive and cumulative, but all scales were administered with a past-week frame. The manuscript does not establish that the Compassion Fatigue-Short Scale is valid for week-to-week fluctuation or that compassion fatigue can plausibly emerge over the selected one-week lags.
issues.quote: Combined, both components of compassion fatigue are progressive and cumulative ... For all scales, participants were prompted to respond about their experiences over the past week.

issues.description: The authors selected the highest-loading items to shorten scales, which can narrow construct coverage and capitalize on prior sample-specific loadings. The reported part-whole correlations are inflated because the short form is embedded in the full scale. This is weak evidence that the shortened and adapted healthcare versions preserve validity.
issues.quote: For each scale, the highest loading items were chosen from reported factor analytic data to maintain a reasonable survey length and achieve internal consistency reliability ... assessed part-whole correlations between the full scales and shortened versions during pilot testing

issues.description: The manuscript says it uses social learning theory, but then immediately describes the stressor-emotion model of CWB as if it were the same model. Social learning theory and the stressor-emotion model make different assumptions and imply different mechanisms. This muddles the theoretical basis for the hypotheses.
issues.quote: To understand how incivility experiences from customers may be impacting employee affect and behavior over time, we utilize social learning theory (Bandura, 1977). This model considers how individuals learn behaviors through observation and modeling of others' actions and their consequences, ultimately shaping counterproductive work behaviors (CWB), such as enacted incivility. Applied to enacted incivility, the general premise of the model suggests that enacted incivility occurs due to a sequence of events where environmental stressors at work lead to enacted incivility through appraisal, perceptions of the stressor, and negative emotions (Spector & Fox, 2005).

issues.description: The compassion fatigue section states that the current study examines coworker incivility, contradicting the rest of the manuscript, which focuses on patient/customer incivility. This suggests conceptual or editing inconsistency in the hypothesized model.
issues.quote: Within the current study, we look specifically at the relationship between experiencing coworker incivility and experiencing a caregiving specific form of job burnout, compassion fatigue.

issues.subcategory: no autoregressive controls for prior construct levels
issues.description: The longitudinal mediation claims are not supported unless prior levels of mediators and outcomes are controlled. The reported regressions predict T3 negative emotions from T2 incivility, T4 compassion fatigue from T3 negative emotions, and T4 enacted incivility from T4 compassion fatigue, but the tables do not show controls for prior negative emotions, compassion fatigue, or enacted incivility. Thus associations may reflect stable between-person differences rather than within-person change over time.
issues.quote: We tested this hypothesis by regressing negative emotions toward patients (T3) onto experienced patient incivility (T2). ... Time 3 negative emotions toward patients were positively related to Time 4 compassion fatigue ... Customer Incivility (T2)  Negative Emotions (T3)  Compassion Fatigue (T4)  Enacted Incivility

issues.description: The study is observational, self-report, and nonrandomized, yet the manuscript repeatedly uses causal language such as “leads to,” “impacts,” and “drives.” Temporal ordering alone does not rule out confounding, reverse causation, stable traits, unit climate, workload, or prior burnout.
issues.quote: These findings suggest that repeated exposure to incivility leads to both poor wellbeing outcomes for the target of incivility and to future enacted incivility.

issues.description: The models appear to include few covariates, mainly work hours, and do not address plausible confounders such as trait negative affectivity, baseline burnout, personality, job role, unit climate, staffing, nurse-patient ratio, patient volume, shift type, workplace violence, psychiatric/delirium caseload, organizational tenure, or recruitment source. These variables could cause both experienced incivility and negative emotions/fatigue/enacted incivility.

The final mediator, compassion fatigue, and the outcome, enacted incivility, are both measured at T4. This prevents establishing temporal precedence for the final mediation path and makes the serial mediation claim ambiguous. Enacted incivility could contribute to compassion fatigue, both could be co-reported due to current mood, or both could reflect a common latent distress factor.
issues.quote: Compassion Fatigue (T4) ... Enacted Incivility (T4) ... Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients

issues.subcategory: incorrect description of serial indirect effect
issues.description: For a serial mediation from experienced incivility to negative emotions to compassion fatigue to enacted incivility, the indirect effect should multiply all component paths in the chain. The manuscript states that it multiplied only the first and last stages, labeled a × d. This is statistically incorrect as written and makes the reported indirect effect difficult to verify.
issues.quote: Here, the indirect effect was estimated by multiplying the first and last stages in the serial mediation process (a × d).

issues.subcategory: inconsistent SE, p-value, and CI for indirect effect
issues.description: The reported Hypothesis 4 indirect effect has B=.06, SE=.04, p<.01, and 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]. If SE=.04, the z/t ratio is about 1.5, not p<.01, and the CI is inconsistent with that SE. Table 2 instead reports SE=.02. This is a substantive reporting/statistical inconsistency for the central effect.
issues.quote: Time 2 experienced patient incivility was indirectly related to Time 4 enacted incivility toward patients (B = .06, SE = .04, p < .01, 95% CI [0.02, 0.10]). ... Customer Incivility  Negative Emotions  Compassion Fatigue  Enacted Incivility | .06** | .02 | 2.58

issues.subcategory: main and supplemental regression estimates conflict
issues.description: The same final-stage predictors are reported with materially different coefficients and standard errors in Table 2 versus the supplemental relative-importance analysis. Table 2 reports negative emotions B=.28, SE=.10 and compassion fatigue B=.57, SE=.17, whereas the supplemental regression reports both as B=.23, SE=.04. The manuscript does not explain whether these are standardized vs unstandardized estimates, different samples, different estimators, or different covariate sets.
issues.quote: T3 Negative Emotions ... .28** | .10 | 2.89 ... T4 Compassion Fatigue ... .57*** | .17 | 3.35 ... experienced incivility (B = -.03, SE = .04, p = .40), negative emotions (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001), and compassion fatigue (B = .23, SE = .04, p < .001).

issues.subcategory: moderated mediation overclaim despite nonsignificant conditional indirect effects
issues.description: The supplemental analyses show that the conditional indirect effects and index of moderated mediation are nonsignificant, but the discussion and practice implications imply that high patient acuity increases risk of the full cascade ending in enacted incivility. The evidence supports moderation only of the first path, not the indirect effect to enacted incivility.
issues.quote: the slopes at low ... medium ... and high levels ... of perceived patient acuity were all non-significant. ... the IMM was non-significant ... Taken together, these results reveal the indirect effect is not conditional upon perceived patient acuity. ... employees experiencing incivility from patients and who have a high perceived patient acuity load are at the highest risk of experiencing increased negative affect and fatigue and, ultimately, engaging in incivility.

issues.subcategory: extreme correlations suggest poor discriminant validity/common method
issues.description: Several correlations among supposedly distinct constructs are extremely high, including T3 negative emotions with T4 enacted incivility r=.94, T4 compassion fatigue with T4 enacted incivility r=.91, and T3 negative emotions with T4 compassion fatigue r=.96. Such correlations suggest construct redundancy, common-method artifacts, response-pattern problems, or multicollinearity, yet the manuscript claims discriminant validity based primarily on CFA fit.
issues.quote: T4 Enacted Incivility | 2.77 | 1.21 | .67 | .69 | .82 | .72 | .36 | -.40 | .82 | .87 | .94 | .91 ... The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable ... and fit the data better than alternative models with fewer factors.

issues.description: The regression and mediation models include predictors that are highly intercorrelated, especially negative emotions and compassion fatigue. Multicollinearity can destabilize coefficients, inflate standard errors, produce suppressor effects, and undermine claims about which mediator is more important. No diagnostics such as VIFs, condition indices, or latent-factor correlations are reported.
issues.quote: T3 Negative Emotions ... T4 Compassion Fatigue ... .96 ... T4 Enacted Incivility ... .94 | .91

issues.description: The confirmatory factor analysis is insufficiently reported. The chi-square label is missing, alternative model specifications are not described, factor loadings and latent correlations are not reported, and no SRMR or residual diagnostics are provided. Given the very high observed correlations, detailed discriminant-validity evidence is essential.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99) and fit the data better than alternative models with fewer factors.

issues.description: The same adapted scales were administered weekly and longitudinal paths are interpreted over time, but the manuscript does not report tests of configural, metric, or scalar invariance across waves. Without invariance, changes or lagged relations may partly reflect changes in measurement properties rather than construct relations.
issues.quote: Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks.

issues.description: The analytic strategy does not clearly specify whether mediation models used observed scale scores or latent variables, the estimator used for path models, how ordinal Likert items were treated outside the CFA, whether robust standard errors were used, how interactions were centered/scaled, or how missing data were handled. These omissions impede replication and evaluation of assumptions.
issues.quote: We then used a Monte Carlo simulation with 20,000 replications ... to construct confidence intervals around the parameter estimates of all indirect effects and the Index of Moderated Mediation (IMM).

issues.subcategory: unjustified wave selection with no preregistration
issues.description: Because identical measures were collected at all four waves, many lag structures were possible: T1→T2→T3, T2→T3→T4, cross-lagged models, autoregressive models, averaged weekly exposure, or within-person models. The manuscript focuses on T2/T3/T4 and does not report preregistration, an analysis plan, or sensitivity analyses across plausible lags. This creates researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks. ... We tested this hypothesis by regressing negative emotions toward patients (T3) onto experienced patient incivility (T2).

issues.subcategory: one-week lag not sufficiently justified for all constructs
issues.description: The manuscript asserts that one-week lags are sufficient and equivalent to longer lags for observing incivility/CWB, but compassion fatigue is described as cumulative and progressive. The proper temporal lag for incivility effects on negative emotions, compassion fatigue, and enacted incivility is not empirically established in this sample, and no lag-sensitivity analyses are reported.
issues.quote: Previous studies have shown that lags spanning this length of time are sufficient for observing emergence of such counterproductive behaviors as incivility and that the observed effects will not meaningfully differ from studies featuring longer periods of time between waves

issues.description: Experienced incivility, emotions, compassion fatigue, acuity, and enacted incivility are all self-reported by the same respondent. Enacted incivility toward patients is socially undesirable and may be underreported or distorted by self-perception. The lack of patient, peer, supervisor, observational, or administrative measures limits validity despite temporal separation.
issues.quote: This study is a four-wave panel longitudinal design that will include administration of self-report online questionnaires ... Four items from the Enacted Incivility Scale ... were used to measure the frequency participants instigated incivility towards their patients.

issues.description: The relative-importance analysis reports percentages summing to 100% and says predictors accounted for those percentages of the variance in enacted incivility. Relative-importance metrics usually apportion explained variance among predictors, not total outcome variance. With highly collinear predictors, these percentages are also unstable and should not be interpreted as showing that compassion fatigue is a stronger causal driver.
issues.quote: The results revealed compassion fatigue, negative emotion, and experienced incivility accounted for 45.1%, 30.8%, and 24.1% of the variance in enacted incivility, respectively.

issues.description: The discussion interprets the relative-importance analysis as evidence that compassion fatigue is a stronger driver of enacted incivility. Relative weights from observational same-time predictors cannot establish causal priority, especially when compassion fatigue and enacted incivility are measured at the same wave and highly correlated.
issues.quote: our results suggest that while the emotion response is an important proximal response to incivility experiences, the subsequent compassion fatigue response is a stronger driver of enacted incivility.

issues.description: The manuscript reports excluding one participant for missing more than 50% of questions but does not state how item-level missingness below that threshold was handled when computing scale scores or running models. This matters for reproducibility and may affect reliability and estimates.
issues.quote: Responses were considered failed data quality checks if they had any of the following characteristics ... missing values exceeded 50% of the questions (n = 1).

issues.description: The moderation model uses only N=244 after missingness, but no a priori power analysis or minimum detectable interaction effect is reported. Interaction and moderated-mediation effects typically require larger samples than main effects; therefore nonsignificant conditional indirect effects may reflect insufficient power, and the significant interaction may be unstable.
issues.quote: Note. N = 244. The sample size was reduced due to missingness on the moderator variable.

issues.description: Table 3 appears misformatted, with duplicated column labels and repeated B columns. This makes it difficult to determine which estimates correspond to which dependent variables and whether significance labels are applied correctly.
issues.quote: Variables | Customer Incivility (T2) | Customer Incivility (T2) | Customer Incivility (T2) | Customer Incivility (T2) | Negative Emotions (T3) | Negative Emotions (T3) | Negative Emotions (T3) | Negative Emotions (T3) | Compassion Fatigue (T4) | Compassion Fatigue (T4) | Compassion Fatigue (T4) | Enacted Incivility (T4) | Enacted Incivility (T4) | Enacted Incivility (T4) ... | B | SE | t | B | B | SE | t | B | B | SE | t | B | SE | t

issues.description: The stated retention rates are rounded or incorrect. For example, 454/458 is approximately 99.1%, not 98%, and 450/454 is also approximately 99.1%, not 98%. Although minor, this contributes to broader concerns about sample-flow accuracy.
issues.quote: n = 458 responded at time 2 (98% retention rate between T1 and T2); n = 454 responded at time 3 (98% retention rate between T2 and T3); and n = 450 responded at time 4 (98% retention rate between T3 and T4).

issues.description: The final sample is 96.64% female, which is more female-skewed than the cited registered-nurse workforce estimate of about 88%. Gender may relate to incivility exposure, reporting, emotional labor, and patient interactions. Generalizations to nurses or service employees more broadly should be cautious.
issues.quote: The majority of respondents were female (96.64%) ... as of 2019, around 88% of registered nurses are women

issues.description: The practice implications infer possible decreased quality of care, but patient care quality, safety, satisfaction, or clinical outcomes were not measured. Enacted incivility is not equivalent to reduced care quality, so this extrapolation is speculative.
issues.quote: Within healthcare, this (combined with high workloads and increased feelings of compassion fatigue) could mean decreased quality care provision.

issues.description: The title and discussion frame the study as incivility begetting incivility, but the design does not identify whether the same patient/family member who enacted incivility later received incivility, nor does it separate interpersonal retaliation from generalized spillover. The measures aggregate across patients and weeks, so direct reciprocity or spiraling cannot be established.
issues.quote: Incivility begets incivility ... The often fleeting or temporary interactions with customers means that retaliatory mechanisms are likely not as informative ... we examine how customer incivility experiences are influencing incivility enactment over time

issues.subcategory: lack of blinding/control for demand characteristics
issues.description: Participants were repeatedly asked about incivility, emotions, fatigue, and their own incivility over four weeks. No blinding or masking of study hypotheses is described. Repeated measurement of conceptually linked constructs may increase demand characteristics or consistency motifs, especially in self-report mediation models.
issues.quote: This study is a four-wave panel longitudinal design that will include administration of self-report online questionnaires ... Identical surveys were administered at each time point across four consecutive weeks.

issues.description: The qualitative pilot had only six participants from personal networks, and the quantitative pilot had 50 MTurk nurses. The manuscript does not report demographic characteristics, verification of eligibility, pilot item statistics beyond part-whole correlations, or how qualitative feedback was systematically analyzed. This limits evaluation of the adapted measures.
issues.quote: We conducted two, independent exploratory pilot studies ... qualitative interviews and focus groups (n = 6) ... quantitative online survey testing (n = 50) ... The qualitative pilot consisted of n = 6 nurses ... recruited from the research team’s personal networks. ... The quantitative pilot consisted of n = 50 nurses ... recruited from MTurk.

issues.subcategory: CFA fit characterized as acceptable despite borderline RMSEA and large chi-square
issues.description: The CFA is described as acceptable despite RMSEA=.08, which is borderline, and a very large chi-square relative to df. The manuscript does not discuss this mixed fit or provide additional diagnostics. Given the centrality of discriminant validity and the extreme observed correlations, the conclusion is insufficiently supported.
issues.quote: The fit of the four-factor model was acceptable (269) = 862.05, RMSEA = .08, CFI = .99, TLI = .99)

issues.description: The manuscript lists items and response scales but does not explicitly state how scale scores were computed, how percentage acuity was transformed to proportions, whether variables were standardized or mean-centered for interactions, or whether reliability was assessed at each wave. This impedes replication and interpretation of unstandardized coefficients.
issues.quote: Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Never) to 5 (Always). ... Table 1 ... T1 Patient Acuity | .54 | .25

issues.subcategory: reverse causation not adequately ruled out
issues.description: Nurses who enact incivility may elicit more negative reactions from patients/families, perceive patients more negatively, or report more experienced incivility. Without reciprocal cross-lagged paths or prior outcome controls, the analyses cannot distinguish patient incivility causing nurse incivility from nurse incivility causing patient incivility or shared reciprocal cycles.
issues.quote: Experiencing incivility, for example, is related to decreased performance, increased deviant behaviors, and increased negative social interactions with others at work ... We therefore propose a two-step process through which experiencing incivility from customers relates to future incivility perpetration
